parts.text:
You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: That's fine. What was the first thing you did when you started work yesterday?

Q3
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: No problem. How would you describe what you do on the airspace desk, in your own words?

Q4
The answer just before it: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. My work serves all customer companies, and I have no business looking into any one company's operations.
The question: When a closure is announced by the authorities, how does it reach you, and what do you do with it?

Q5
The answer just before it: I don't know how closures reach me. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
The question: Can you give me an example of a recent closure and what "disruption" meant in that case?

Q6
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When you say "how much disruption across customers", what would you need to be able to tell, or know?

Q7
The answer just before it: I want to know how much disruption a closure caused across customers when it is entered.
The question: Thinking about the last few months, what was the worst day on the desk?

Q8
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Is there anything in your work today that you check by hand because you don't fully trust it?

Q9
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Who do you pass your work on to, once the airspace picture is updated?

Q10
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What would worry you most about a new service handling the airspace picture?

Q11
The answer just before it: The service runs on a single server, and it is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying. It also occasionally crashes, though the companies accept a few minutes of interruption.
The question: When the service restarts or crashes while drones are flying, what are you afraid could go wrong for you?

Q12
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Right after something has gone wrong with the airspace picture, what's the first thing you'd need to know?

Q13
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: You said you have no business looking into any one company's operations. Where does that line fall for you when you look at disruption from a closure?

Q14
The answer just before it: I keep the shared picture of the airspace for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations, as each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
The question: Once you know how much disruption a closure caused, who do you tell or what do you do with it?

Q15
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Who asks you to change the corridors or zones, and how does that request reach you?

Q16
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When did you last enter a closure, and what happened afterwards?

Q17
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: You mentioned the service occasionally crashes. What happens on your side when it does?

Q18
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Is there anything about your work on the airspace desk that I haven't asked about but should know?

Q19
The answer just before it: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which consists of the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations, because each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
The question: How would you tell whether a closure caused a lot of disruption or very little?
